overview: Baekje held the southwest of the Korean peninsula and was the most refined of the Three Kingdoms, trading by sea with China and Japan. Its monks, scholars and craftsmen carried Buddhism, Chinese learning and temple architecture to the Yamato court.

items.text: Sea routes linked Baekje to the southern Chinese dynasties and to Japan, and possibly further south.
King Seong sent a Buddha image, sutras and monks to the Yamato court, the official introduction of Buddhism to Japan; Japanese sources date it to 538 or 552.
The Baekje smile, the gentle expression of its stone and bronze Buddhas, as on the rock-cut triad at Seosan.
Gilt-bronze Buddhas, reliquaries and roof tiles stamped with lotus designs.
The Gilt-bronze Incense Burner of Baekje, found at Neungsan-ri in 1993, a mountain of peaks, musicians and animals on a lotus base.
The monk Marananta arrived from Eastern Jin and the court adopted Buddhism, building temples and monastic communities.
Confucian learning and the Chinese classics were taught to the aristocracy; Baekje scholars such as Wang In took the classics to Japan.
The Baekje Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.
Baekje's transmission of Buddhism, writing and craft shaped early Japanese civilization.

fall.text: A Silla army and a Tang fleet took the capital Sabi in 660; a restoration movement was crushed at the Baekgang river in 663, and Silla absorbed the land by 676.
